summary:
EARTHSONIC: The Earth Information Jukebox

EarthSonic is an accessibility-first platform that turns NASA's Earth observations into music, allowing people to hear what is happening on our planet. It transforms real climate and satellite data, including temperature changes and wildfire patterns, into sounds by manipulating pitch, speed, and volume based on data

EarthSonic addresses the challenge of making scientific information accessible to everyone, especially people who are blind or have low vision. It combines an interactive 3D globe, location-based soundscapes, an AI voice assistant, and Braille keyboard compatibility allowing users to explore the planet independently without relying on sight or a mouse.

EarthSonic matters because access to science should never depend on the ability to see. It gives everyone a new way to experience, understand, and connect with our changing planet.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

At its heart, EARTHSONIC: The Earth Information Jukebox turns NASA’s Earth Information Center observations into music you can actually listen to and learn from. Rather than looking at static charts or watching satellite videos passively, users can literally hear the pulse and rhythms of our planet.

The system works through a transparent scientific mapping engine built with Tone.js and the native Web Audio API:

  • Pitch and Melodic Harmony: Reflects absolute numerical values. In climate datasets like NASA GISTEMP (1880–2024), rising temperatures push melodies up through carefully tuned harmonic scales (Dorian, Lydian, and Phrygian modes).
  • Tempo and Rhythmic Pulse: Governed by the rate of change—rapidly shifting environmental events (like the rapid expansion of Northern California’s Dixie Fire) produce accelerated percussion beats.
  • Timbre and Texture: Dictated by surface complexity and motion flux. Oceanic currents produce wide, filtered ambient washes, while turbulent weather or lightning strikes trigger sharp, resonant synth strikes.
  • Spatial Stereo Panning: Coordinates on Earth are projected across the stereo field, letting users naturally perceive whether an event is unfolding in the Western or Eastern hemisphere.

Users can choose any coordinate on Earth using an interactive 3D globe or 2D map, search for specific biomes (from the Amazon Rainforest to the Arctic Ocean), or scrub through 144 years of planetary history. For full transparency, an interactive "Why am I hearing this?" panel breaks down the exact math behind every note, chord, and drumbeat in real time.

ACCESSIBILITY, BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The primary motivation behind EarthSonic is genuine independence for blind and low-vision individuals.

Today, AI chatbots and screen readers attempt to summarize visual graphs with captions like "the trend line goes up." But that completely strips away the richness of the data. An AI cannot adequately describe the intricate spatial swirl of Gulf Stream eddies, the gradual crawl of temperature anomalies across continents, or the density of tropical lightning. For visually impaired users, science has long been locked behind a visual wall.

EarthSonic replaces that secondary, mediated description with direct experience. By translating real data into sound, a blind user can sit down at a laptop, choose a place on Earth, press play, and analyze the planetary trends for themselves—at their own pace, with complete autonomy.

For educators and sighted students, this dual-sensory approach also uncovers patterns and cyclical anomalies that the human eye frequently glazes over in a busy line graph.

TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES AND ARCHITECTURE

We built EarthSonic to be lightweight, responsive, and completely friction-free—no bulky downloads, no high-end gaming GPUs required:

  • Frontend Framework: React 18 with TypeScript and Vite, styled using Tailwind CSS for clean contrast and responsiveness.
    • Perkins-Style Braille Input: Custom keyboard driver mapping the six Braille dots to F, D, S, J, K, L, allowing users familiar with mechanical Braillers to navigate tabs, toggle playback, and control audio via simultaneous chords.
    • Spoken TTS Onboarding: Integrated Web Speech API that sonically greets users on page open and outlines the primary keyboard and Braille controls.
    • AI Voice Assistant: An embedded voice assistant supporting natural-language requests (such as "Take me to the Amazon" or "What am I listening to?") triggered by a long spacebar press.
  • Data Sources and APIs: Direct integration with official NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) APIs (EIC gallery 40467, Dixie Fire 4993, Climate Spiral 5190, GISTEMP 5425, ECCO2 oceans), accompanied by Python preprocessing pipelines and built-in client-side rate limiting.

CREATIVITY AND THOUGHTFUL DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

Throughout development, our team prioritized three core considerations:

  1. Aesthetic Musicality vs. Scientific Accuracy: Data sonification often sounds like harsh Geiger-counter clicks or abrasive noise. We took great care to ground our synthesizers in music theory, selecting scales and warm reverberation that make listening a meditative, enjoyable experience without distorting the underlying data points.
  2. Inclusive Control Schemes: We recognized that not everyone navigates the web the same way. We integrated three distinct interaction tiers: standard visual mouse/touch, complete single-key keyboard shortcuts (with spacebar duration sensing), and a dedicated 6-dot Perkins Braille chord system.
  3. Hardware Accessibility and Future Roadmap: We engineered this V1.0 web build to run smoothly on modest school laptops and older hardware. Looking forward to Version 2.0 (targeted for December 2026), we are designing a dedicated tactile hardware ring that will allow users to navigate Earth observations and feel vibrations directly on their fingertips—eliminating screen and keyboard dependency altogether.
